title: Syllabus
text:
Catalog description
IMSE 456. Program and Project Management. 3 Credits. Integrated approaches to managing engineering, technology and business projects, addressing the project management lifecycle including initiating, planning, executing, controlling and closing. Additional topics include program management, portfolio management, and applying principles in a business environment. Prereq or Coreq: Junior standing. Dual-listing: IMSE 656.

title: Syllabus
text:
How this course runs
Two sessions a week, and they do different jobs.
Tuesday is concept. The chapter’s ideas, and usually a short case or discussion with a decision in it. You leave knowing what is due.
Thursday is studio, and it is hands-on and individual. Every student works at their own machine on the same three movements:

Build — 25 minutes. Work the concept out yourself first — by hand, in a spreadsheet, in a notebook, or with AI help. No professional software yet.
Use — 20 minutes. Do the same thing in the real tool: ProjectLibre, Smartsheet, Taiga or Power BI.
Reconcile — 15 minutes. Compare the two. If the numbers match, say so and say why you would trust them. If they do not match exactly, explain how they differ and why — a different definition, a different assumption, a rounding choice, or a mistake in one of them. Either answer is fine. Not looking is not.

Then save and upload. Save your own copy to your NDSU Google Drive or OneDrive, and upload the file to Blackboard before you leave the room. The saved copy is yours to keep; the uploaded one is what gets graded.

How studios are graded
Complete or incomplete. A studio is complete when every item on its checklist is present in the file you uploaded. That is the whole rubric — and you get written feedback on what you submitted.







Complete
All checklist items present · reconciliation paragraph written · uploaded to Blackboard


Incomplete
Something on the checklist is missing



Getting a different answer from the tool does not make a studio incomplete. Not explaining the difference does.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
Project management as it is actually practised: the quantitative core — work breakdown, critical path, PERT, resource levelling, crashing, earned value — alongside adaptive delivery and flow metrics, with hybrid treated as the normal real-world case.
AI runs through every week. You will use it to draft project artifacts — work breakdowns, risk registers, status reports, schedules — and then check what it produced against the real tool and against your own work. In the final project your team builds a small AI-assisted project-management workflow and writes about it publicly.

title: Syllabus
text:
Course objectives
By the end of the course you can:

Decide which delivery approach fits a given project and defend the choice against a specific alternative.
Build and interpret the core quantitative artifacts: WBS, CPM network, PERT distribution, resource-levelled schedule, crash analysis, EVM report.
Run the adaptive artifacts: product backlog, sprint mechanics, cumulative flow diagram, Little’s Law.
Read the evidence critically — distinguish a base rate from a vendor statistic.
Diagnose a failing project and propose interventions ranked by expected effect, not by convention.
Use AI to produce project artifacts, check them, and describe clearly where it helped and where it was wrong.


Additional expectations for students enrolled in IMSE 656
Students enrolled under the graduate number complete the same components at a higher level of expectation:

Studio assignments require the reconciliation paragraph to cite the mechanism, not only the symptom — which algorithm or formula choice produces this difference, with a reference.
Final project includes a short methods justification: why you chose the delivery approach, estimating method and control mechanism you did.
Final presentation includes a five-minute defence against a challenge drawn from the counter-evidence for the position taken.

text:
Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
Generative AI use in this course is permitted and expected, within the parameters below. This section is the course’s AI policy under NDSU Policy 335: Code of Academic Responsibility and Conduct. Use outside these parameters is academic dishonesty and is handled under that policy.
Much of this course is about using these tools well and knowing when they are wrong. That is a learning objective, not a concession.

Approved tools
Gemini, Google Antigravity, the Gemini API supplied through the course notebook, and Microsoft 365 Copilot are approved for all permitted uses without further request. Any other general-purpose assistant is approved on the same terms provided you name it in your disclosure. Anything that is not a general-purpose assistant — a tool that completes assignments for you, or a service you would have to send course material to — ask first.
Every student has access to Gemini and Antigravity, and the instructor supplies API keys to anyone who needs them, so no graded work in this course depends on being able to buy a subscription.


How much AI, on which assessment
Each assessment carries a level from the Generative AI Acceptable Use Scale (Perkins et al., 2024). The level is repeated on every lab sheet and assignment so you never have to guess.








Assessment
Level
What that means here




Midterm examination

Closed book, closed notes, no computers or phones. The reasoning this tests is the reasoning you need when the tool is unavailable or wrong.


Conceptual assignments (CA1–CA8)

These are quizzes. Use AI freely to study — the Tutor prompts in AI Studio are built for it — but not while the assessment is open.

Generate freely, including the code. Every quantitative result arrives with the check that proves it, and the reconciliation paragraph must be your own reasoning.

You are required to build and run an agent that maintains a live project artifact, and to report what it got wrong and how you caught it.





How to disclose
Append this to any submission where AI was used. It takes two minutes and its absence is what turns permitted use into a violation.

AI acknowledgement. Tool used: [name]. What I used it for: [e.g. drafting the WBS]. Prompt or transcript: [link or screenshot]. What I changed after reading its output: [edits]. What it got wrong: [or “nothing I found”].



The requirements, in short

Acknowledge any significant AI contribution in submissions.
Verify all AI-generated content for accuracy.
Use AI ethically; violations constitute academic dishonesty.
AI is forbidden for quizzes and tests — the midterm and the conceptual assignments.



Data, confidentiality and privacy
This matters more here than in most courses, because your final project involves a real organization’s information.

Do not put a partner organization’s confidential information into any AI tool. Costs, contracts, customer data, unreleased plans, anything they asked you to protect. Generalize the problem or use synthetic numbers instead. If you are unsure whether something is confidential, it is.
Do not put anyone’s personal information into an AI tool — classmates’, a partner’s staff, your own beyond what you would post publicly.
Do not upload another student’s work. Their submissions are their educational records.
If a partner asks for a written commitment about AI use, bring it to the instructor before you agree to anything. Do not sign on behalf of NDSU.

title: Syllabus
text:
Instructor use of AI — disclosure
You are being asked to label, verify and own your AI use. The same standard applies to the person teaching you, so here is exactly how AI was used to build this course.
What AI did. Working from my own outlines, notes and the textbook’s chapter structure, I used generative AI to help organize the course: to sequence the sixteen weeks against Larson’s chapters and argue about where the displacement should fall; to draft and edit lecture notes, the mini-cases you read on Tuesdays, and the studio lab sheets you work from on Thursdays; to generate the studio datasets and compute every answer key programmatically; to draft rubrics and the “done looks like” checklists; and to build this website.
What AI did not do, and will not do.

It does not grade you. No AI system assigns or recommends a mark in this course.
Your work is not uploaded to any third-party AI system, for grading or for any other purpose. Your submissions are educational records under FERPA and they stay in Blackboard.
It does not decide anything. Every sequencing choice, assessment weight, rubric criterion and final grade is mine.

What I verify. Every factual claim, empirical figure and citation in these materials is checked against a primary source before it is published — the sources are listed in AI Studio so you can check them too. Every numerical answer key is computed in code rather than by hand, precisely because a hand-worked key is where errors hide and an error in a key is worse than an error in a lecture.
Where you can see it. This site is public and so is the repository that builds it. If you want to see how a course is actually assembled, including the parts a model drafted, you can read the source. That transparency is the point: I am asking you to show your work, so I show mine.
If AI use in this course changes — a new tool, a new use — it will be announced on Blackboard and this section updated. If you think something here was AI-generated and is wrong, tell me. You will be right often enough to make it worth asking, and finding it is exactly the skill this course is trying to build.

title: Studio 1 · Chapter 1 review questions
text:
Study loop for this week
Run this before you read the notes, and again after. It is not graded; it is the fastest way to find out what you have wrong.
Be my tutor on the difference between a project and an operation. Ask me
one question at a time. Don't lecture. Start by making me state the test,
then hand me cases that break it — a film studio, a release train, a
refinery shutdown — until I stop treating it as a fact about the world.
See AI Studio for the Editor and Roommate prompts and the full loop.

title: AI Studio
text:
Project management is one of the first disciplines where the routine artifacts — charters, work breakdowns, risk registers, status reports — can be drafted by a machine in seconds. That does not make the discipline easier. It moves the difficulty from production to judgement: someone still has to know whether the WBS is complete, whether the estimate is defensible, and whether the status report is telling the truth.
This course teaches that judgement by making you use the tools constantly and hold them to account every time.

title: AI Studio
text:
Build → Use → Reconcile
Every Thursday studio runs the same three movements, and the AI sits inside the first one. You build the tool — often by directing an agent to write it — then use the professional software on the same data, then explain where the two disagree.
This is the entire argument for teaching project management to engineers rather than leaving it to a certification. A course that only teaches ProjectLibre produces students who can operate a tool until the version changes. A course that only teaches the mathematics produces students who have never seen a resource histogram. Building it and then using it produces the one capability that transfers: knowing when the tool is wrong.

title: AI Studio
text:
The study loop

The five roles
Five roles, five different jobs. The framework is Sandeep Swadia’s “University in a Box” from How To Become Dangerously Self-Educated (with AI). None of it is graded — it is the fastest way to find out what you have wrong before an assignment does it for you.








Role
Its job
Where you meet it




Adviser
Sets destination, baseline, sequencing
The syllabus and the schedule


Librarian
Curates credible sources, defends against distraction
The source shelf below, and per-week readings


Tutor
Asks one question at a time, finds the gap, does not lecture
“Tutor check” in every week’s notes; the per-week prompt at the foot of each lab sheet


Editor
Challenges logic, finds weak arguments, cuts repetition
“Editor challenge” — a defensible-sounding claim you have to attack


Roommate
Brings perspective from an unrelated field
“Roommate link” — a cross-domain analogy that transfers structure, not vocabulary




Tutor prompt
Be my tutor on [TOPIC] in project management. Ask me one question at a
time. Don't lecture me. Find the gap in my understanding. Be precise.

When I get something wrong, don't correct me immediately — ask a follow-up
that makes me find the error myself. Only explain after I've tried twice.

Two commands I'll use: "teach me" means give me the explanation now; "test
me" means switch to harder questions on the same topic.
For exam preparation, the retrieval variant — mixed questions drawn from all prior weeks, not the current one. Mixing is what makes retrieval practice work.


Editor prompt
Attack what I just wrote. Find the weakest link in the argument, the claim
that isn't supported, and the place where I've confused a definition with
a conclusion. Be specific and be harsh. Don't tell me what's good about it.


Roommate prompt
I've just learned [CONCEPT] in project management. You work in a completely
different field. Where does this same structure show up in your world, and
what does your version know that mine doesn't?

title: AI Studio
text:
The source shelf
Everything else is optional reading. Load these into a single grounded workspace and make the assistant answer from the shelf, not from the open web.
Standards — look at them; do not memorize them.

PMI, A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK Guide) — Eighth Edition, November 2025 — https://www.pmi.org/standards/pmbok
Schwaber & Sutherland, The Scrum Guide, November 2020 — https://scrumguides.org
Beck et al., Manifesto for Agile Software Development, 2001 — https://agilemanifesto.org
ISO 21502:2020, Project, programme and portfolio management — Guidance on project management

Empirical anchors — the papers this course actually argues from.

Gemino, Horner Reich & Serrador (2021), “Agile, Traditional, and Hybrid Approaches to Project Success”, Project Management Journal. 477 projects.
Serrador & Pinto (2015), “Does Agile work? — A quantitative analysis of agile project success”, IJPM. 1,002 projects.
Koch et al. (2023), “The affective, behavioural and cognitive outcomes of agile project management: A preliminary meta-analysis”, JOOP. Pre-registered; k = 41, N = 73,825.
Young & Jordan (2008), “Top management support: mantra or necessity?”; Young & Poon (2013), IJPM.
Batselier & Vanhoucke (2015), “Empirical Evaluation of Earned Value Management Forecasting Accuracy”, JCEM. 51 real projects.
Flyvbjerg (2021), “Top Ten Behavioral Biases in Project Management”, PMJ. Base rates from 2,062 projects.
Love, Ika et al. (2019), “The cost performance of transportation projects: The fallacy of the Planning Fallacy account”, TR Part A. The counter-case.
Eveleens & Verhoef (2010), “The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures”, IEEE Software 27(1):30–36.







The two failure modes



The model agrees with you. Every prompt above is written to make the assistant adversarial, because the default behaviour is accommodation. If your Editor pass comes back mostly positive, the prompt didn’t take — re-run it with “you were too generous; find three more problems and be harsher.”
The model invents a citation. Ask for a source and you will often get a plausible-looking one that does not exist, or a real paper with the wrong finding attached. Anything you are going to put in a report, verify against the actual document. This is the entire reason the Librarian is a separate step rather than something you do inline.

title: AI Studio
text:
The weekly cycle
Roughly 60–90 minutes per chapter, outside class. Not graded.
1. TUTOR (diagnostic)  — 10 min — what do I already wrongly believe?
2. Read the module     — 20 min — notes + one primary source
3. TUTOR (voice)       — 20 min — one question at a time, no lecturing
4. Write something     — 15 min — a plan, an argument, a worked problem
5. EDITOR              — 10 min — attack what I wrote
6. ROOMMATE            —  5 min — where else does this structure appear?
7. TUTOR (retrieval)   —  5 min — mixed questions from all prior weeks
Steps 4 and 5 do the work. The Tutor finds gaps; producing something and having it attacked is what closes them. A loop that stops after step 3 feels productive and mostly isn’t.

title: Final Project
text: Teams of four or five run a genuine project-management engagement with an outside organization across the semester. Ten teams, formed by Week 3. Not a case study, not a simulation: a real scope, a real sponsor, a real constraint you did not choose.

title: Final Project
text:
Why a partner organization
Everything difficult about this discipline comes from the parts you do not control. A classroom project has a scope you invented, a sponsor who is your instructor, and no cost of being wrong. A partner organization supplies what the exercise otherwise lacks — requirements that shift, a stakeholder whose interest conflicts with yours, and information you have to go and ask for.
The engagement is small on purpose. You are not being asked to deliver the project. You are being asked to manage a defined slice of it and to produce the artifacts that management requires.

title: Final Project
text:
Finding a partner






FP0 is due Friday 11 September



Start looking now. If your team is struggling to find a partner, talk to the instructor early rather than late.


What counts as a partner. Any organization outside this course with a real, bounded piece of work in the next three months: a local manufacturer, a campus unit, a non-profit, a research lab, a student organization with a budget, a startup, a family business. It does not need to be an engineering project.
What you need from them.

One named contact willing to spend roughly 30 minutes every other week with your team.
A bounded scope with a start and an end inside the semester.
Permission to describe the project in a report and a presentation — see confidentiality below.

Where to look. Your own employer or internship; a faculty member’s lab; NDSU facilities, events, or student affairs; the Fargo-Moorhead non-profit sector; a family or friend’s business. Ask early — the request is small and most organizations say yes.

title: Final Project
text:
Confidentiality and intellectual property
Some partners will share information they would not want published. Handle it properly:

Default to public. If nothing sensitive is involved, your report is a normal academic document.
If the partner asks for confidentiality, tell the instructor at FP0. Your report can be marked confidential, read only by the instructor, and excluded from any public archive. Your presentation can be given with figures anonymized.
Never sign anything on behalf of NDSU. If a partner asks your team to sign an NDA, stop and contact the instructor. Students may sign personally only after that conversation.
The partner owns their data. You own your analysis. Say so in writing, in an email, at the start — a two-sentence email now prevents an ugly conversation in December.

title: Final Project
text:
The AI requirement
From FP2 onward, AI is part of how your team runs the project, not an add-on. Use it to draft and maintain at least one artifact — the schedule, the risk register, or the status report — and keep a short record of what you asked it and what you changed.

The Medium article
Each team publishes one article on Medium describing the AI-assisted project-management workflow you built. Roughly 1,000–1,500 words, written for a working professional rather than for your instructor.
Cover four things:

The pipeline. What your team did with AI, step by step — which tool, at which stage, on which artifact. A diagram or screenshots help.
What worked. Where it genuinely saved time or caught something you would have missed.
What it got wrong, with a concrete example. Every workflow that runs for six weeks produces at least one. A piece claiming otherwise is a piece whose authors were not checking.
What you would do differently if you ran the same project again.

Submit the published link with FP4. This is a public, citable artifact with your name on it — it is worth writing well, and it is the part of this course you can show an employer.






Point 3 is graded generously



Finding where the AI was wrong is not a failure of the work; it is the work. What loses marks is having no way you would have noticed.

title: Final Project
text:
Final report structure
Roughly 3,000–4,000 words plus appendices. Sections in whatever order serves the argument, but all present:

The project, the partner, and what success meant to them — on which dimensions, per Week 1.
Delivery approach chosen, and the alternative rejected, with the reason — per Week 12.
Scope: charter and WBS, with what changed and why.
Schedule and cost: the baseline, the actuals, and where they diverged.
Risk: the register, and the risk that materialized or the one you were most wrong about.
Your AI workflow, and the link to your published Medium article.
What you would do differently, ranked by expected effect rather than by convention.

IMSE 656 students additionally include a methods justification: the choice of delivery approach, estimating method, and control mechanism defended against the empirical literature, with citations to the source shelf.

A good time to be reading this

text:
More than a set of tools
Project management gives people a powerful set of tools to plan, implement and manage activities to accomplish specific objectives.

But it is more than that:

A contact sport that requires building collaborative relationships among a diverse cast of stakeholders.

Accountants · lawyers · administrators · scientists · contractors · coaches · public health officials · teachers · community advocates.

For some the work is project driven — cases for lawyers, audits for accountants, events for artists, renovations for contractors.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: For others, a small but critical part
text:
For others, a small but critical part

A teacher with four classes a day, coaching a national debate team
A store manager developing an employee retention programme
A sales exec launching daily deals into a new city
A public health official organising a Homeless Youth Connect event


Not a title. A job requirement.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The skill transfers

It is hard to think of a profession or a career path that would not benefit from being good at managing projects.

Project management fundamentals are universal.
Each person is likely to experience three to four career changes.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: And it shows up in the classroom
text:
And it shows up in the classroom
Twenty years ago: one or two classes, primarily for engineers.
Today: multiple sections — engineers supplemented by marketing, MIS and finance, plus oceanography, health sciences, computer sciences and liberal arts.
Employers are looking for graduates with project management skills.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: What do these have in common?
text:
What do these have in common?

Millions Watch World Cup Finals
Citywide WiFi System Set to Go Live
Hospitals Respond to New Healthcare Reforms
Apple’s New iPhone Hits the Market
City Receives Stimulus Funds to Expand Light Rail System


All of these events are projects.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The definition

A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.

Like most organisational efforts, the major goal is to satisfy a customer’s need.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Five characteristics



#





1
An established objective


2
A defined lifespan with a beginning and an end


3
Usually several departments and professionals


4
Typically something never done before


5
Specific time, cost and performance requirements

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
1 · An established objective
A 12-storey apartment complex by January 1.
Version 2.0 of a software package as quickly as possible.
This singular purpose is often lacking in daily organisational life, where workers perform repetitive operations each day.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
2 · A defined endpoint
Contrary to the ongoing duties of traditional jobs.
Instead of staying in one job, individuals move from project to project, working with different groups of people.
After installing a security system, an IT engineer may be assigned to develop a database for a different client.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
3 · Combined effort of specialists
Unlike work segmented by functional speciality.
Engineers · financial analysts · marketing professionals · quality control specialists.
Instead of separate offices under separate managers, they work together under the guidance of a project manager.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
4 · Nonroutine, with unique elements
Not either/or — a matter of degree.
An electric automobile, or two rovers on Mars: previously unsolved problems and breakthrough technology.

Even basic construction projects with established routines require some degree of customisation that makes them unique.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
5 · Time, cost and performance
Projects are evaluated according to accomplishment, cost and time spent.
These triple constraints impose a higher degree of accountability than is typically found in most jobs.

And they name the primary function: balancing the trade-offs among time, cost and performance while ultimately satisfying the customer.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
What a project is not







Routine, repetitive
Project




Taking class notes
Writing a term paper


Entering sales receipts
Setting up a sales kiosk for a meeting


Responding to a supply-chain request
Developing a supply-chain information system


Practising scales on the piano
Writing a new piano piece


Routine manufacture of a music player
Designing one that stores 10,000 songs

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: Why the distinction earns its keep
text:
Why the distinction earns its keep
Too often resources can be used up on daily operations, which may not contribute to the longer-range organisation strategies that require innovative new products.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Program versus project

A program is a group of related projects designed to accomplish a common goal over an extended period of time.

Each project within a program has a project manager.
The major differences lie in scale and time span. Program goals are closely related to broad strategic organisation goals.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: Predictable changes in effort and focus
text:
Predictable changes in effort and focus
Many life-cycle models are unique to an industry or project type.
New software development: definition · design · code · integration/test · maintenance.
A generic cycle has four stages.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
1 · Defining
Specifications of the project are defined.
Project objectives are established.
Teams are formed.
Major responsibilities are assigned.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
2 · Planning
The level of effort increases.
Plans are developed to determine what the project will entail, when it will be scheduled, whom it will benefit, what quality level should be maintained, and what the budget will be.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
3 · Executing
A major portion of the project work — physical and mental.
The physical product is produced: a bridge, a report, a software program.

Time, cost and specification measures are used for control. On schedule? On budget? Meeting specifications? What are the forecasts? What revisions are necessary?

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
4 · Closing
Three activities:

Delivering the project product to the customer — customer training, transferring documents
Redeploying project resources — releasing equipment and materials, finding new assignments for team members
Post-project review — assessing performance and capturing lessons learned

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The project manager
Project managers are often stars in their organisation and well compensated.
They develop, or are given, a project charter or scope statement defining the objectives and parameters of the project.
They work with others to create a schedule and budget that guide execution — and must understand project priorities so they can make independent decisions.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Traditional PM assumes predictability
Traditional project management focuses on thorough planning up front.
Planning requires predictability. Managers must understand what is to be accomplished and how to do it.
Building a bridge, engineers draw upon proven technology and design principles.

Not all projects enjoy such predictability.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Project uncertainty
Uncertainty varies according to two things:

The extent the project scope (What) is known and stable
The extent the technology (How) is known and proven


Predictable → unpredictable → unknown.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Where planning works
Bridges · product extensions · events · marketing campaigns.
Well-established scopes, proven technology — which provides predictability for effective planning.

When scope and/or technology is not fully known, plan-driven methods suffer.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The cost of ignoring it
$81 billion — spent by American firms and agencies on cancelled software projects, 1995 (Standish Group)
> $2 trillion — cost of poor software quality in the U.S., 2021, from unsuccessful projects, software failure, and inferior quality legacy systems (Krasner, 2022)

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Rolling wave
An incremental, iterative process.
Instead of planning everything up front, the scope evolves. The final design and outcome is not known in great detail, and is continuously developed through incremental iterations — waves.
Iterations typically last one to four weeks.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Each iteration
Makes tangible progress — defining a key requirement, solving a technical problem, creating features to demonstrate to the customer.
At the end, progress is reviewed, adjustments are made, a new cycle begins.

Each new iteration subsumes the work of the previous ones until the project is complete and the customer satisfied.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Agile in one line
Active collaboration between the project team and customer representatives · breaking projects into small functional pieces · adapting to changing requirements.
Agile works best in small teams of four to eight members.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Not simply either/or
Agile up front in the defining phase to establish specifications and requirements.
Traditional methods to plan, execute and close.
Agile also used to address certain technical issues while most of the work is managed traditionally.

Hybrid project management is the name for this blending.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
section: Compression of the product life cycle
text:
Compression of the product life cycle
High-tech product life cycles now average six months to three years. Only 30 years ago, 10 to 15 years was not uncommon.

Rule of thumb: a six-month project delay can cost 33 percent of product revenue share.
Speed becomes a competitive advantage.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Knowledge explosion
Building a road 30 years ago was somewhat simple.
Today: materials, specifications, codes, aesthetics, equipment, required specialists — every area more complex.
Hard to find a new product without at least one microchip. The same is likely true for AI.

Project management has emerged as the key discipline for integrating divergent technologies.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Triple bottom line
Planet · people · profit.
Businesses can no longer simply focus on maximising profit to the detriment of the environment and society.
Reducing carbon imprints and using renewable resources are realised through effective project management — a high LEED certification is often an objective in its own right.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Small projects, big problems
Hundreds of projects implemented concurrently — a multiproject environment.
Sharing and prioritising resources across a portfolio is a major challenge for senior management.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Why small projects hide

They carry the same or more risk as large projects
They are perceived as low-impact — they don’t demand scarce resources or money
Because so many run concurrently and each impact seems small, measuring inefficiency is usually nonexistent
They soon add up to large sums; customers and millions of dollars are lost each year


Hidden costs not measured in the accounting system.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
Managing projects is multidimensional



Technical
Sociocultural




Scope · WBS
Leadership

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The technical dimension
Project management methodology: planning, scheduling, controlling.
Scope statements link the project and customer, and facilitate planning and control.

Think of the WBS as a database, not a diagram — it links every level of the organisation to every deliverable and every piece of work, down to individual tasks.
Because the links are built in, a change anywhere can be traced back to whatever caused it. That traceability is the payoff.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The sociocultural dimension
Where planning is orderly, implementation is messy, frequently contradictory, often paradoxical.
Build a culture that keeps people working together and invested — and that surfaces problems early enough to act on.

Things rarely go as planned. Steer back on track, or alter direction when necessary.

title: Week 1 — Modern Project Management
text:
The social network
Build the social network deliberately — across stakeholders who hold different standards, are committed to different things, and see the same project from incompatible angles.

Neither half covers for the other.
Produce a plan and a budget — and orchestrate people you mostly do not control.

section: Where the project approach came from, and where it went
text:
Where the project approach came from, and where it went
The project approach has long been the style of doing business in the construction industry, the U.S. Department of Defense, Hollywood, and big consulting firms. It has now spread to all avenues of work.
Today project teams carry out everything from port expansions to hospital restructuring to upgrading information systems. They are creating next-generation fuel-efficient vehicles, developing sustainable sources of energy, and exploring the farthest reaches of outer space.
The impact is most profound in high-tech industries, where the new folk heroes are young professionals whose Herculean efforts lead to the constant flow of new hardware and software products.
Project management is not limited to the private sector. It is a vehicle for doing good deeds and solving social problems — providing emergency aid to areas hit by natural disasters, devising a strategy for reducing crime and drug abuse within a city, or organising a community effort to renovate a public playground. All would and do benefit from the application of modern project management techniques.

Other countries are increasingly spending more on projects. Millions of people around the world consider project management the major task in their profession.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
section: Most people who manage projects never hold the title
text:
Most people who manage projects never hold the title
Many people who excel at managing projects never have the title project manager. They include accountants, lawyers, administrators, scientists, contractors, coaches, public health officials, teachers and community advocates whose success depends upon being able to lead and manage project work.
For some, the very nature of the work is project driven — cases for lawyers, audits for accountants, events for artists, renovations for contractors.
For others, projects are a small but critical part of the work:

A high school teacher who teaches four classes a day is responsible for coaching a group of students to compete in a national debate competition.
A store manager who oversees daily operations is charged with developing an employee retention programme.
A sales account executive is given the additional assignment of team lead to launch daily deals into a new city.
A public health official who manages a clinic is also responsible for organising a Homeless Youth Connect event.

For these and others, project management is not a title but a critical job requirement.

It is hard to think of a profession or a career path that would not benefit from being good at managing projects.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The skill transfers
Not only is project management critical to most careers, the skill set is transferable across most businesses and professions. Project management fundamentals are universal. The same methodology used to develop a new product can be adapted to create new services, organise events, refurbish ageing operations, and so forth.
In a world where it is estimated that each person is likely to experience three to four career changes, managing projects is a talent worthy of development.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
section: And it shows up in the classroom
text:
And it shows up in the classroom
Twenty years ago, major universities offered one or two classes in project management, primarily for engineers. Today most universities offer multiple sections, with the core group of engineers supplemented by business students majoring in marketing, management information systems (MIS) and finance, as well as students from oceanography, health sciences, computer sciences and liberal arts.
These students are finding that their exposure to project management provides distinct advantages when it comes time to look for jobs. More and more employers are looking for graduates with project management skills.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The definition
The Project Management Institute provides the following definition [4]:

A project is a temporary endeavour undertaken to create a unique product, service, or result.

Like most organisational efforts, the major goal of a project is to satisfy a customer’s need. Beyond that fundamental similarity, the characteristics of a project help differentiate it from other endeavours of the organisation.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The five characteristics







#
Characteristic




1
An established objective


2
A defined lifespan with a beginning and an end


3
Usually, the involvement of several departments and professionals


4
Typically, doing something that has never been done before


5
Specific time, cost, and performance requirements



First — a defined objective. Whether it is constructing a 12-storey apartment complex by January 1 or releasing version 2.0 of a specific software package as quickly as possible. This singular purpose is often lacking in daily organisational life, where workers perform repetitive operations each day.
Second — a defined endpoint. Because there is a specified objective, projects have an endpoint, contrary to the ongoing duties and responsibilities of traditional jobs. Instead of staying in one job, individuals often move from project to project, working with different groups of people. For example, after helping to install a security system, an IT engineer may be assigned to develop a database for a different client.
Third — combined effort of specialists. Unlike much organisational work that is segmented according to functional speciality, projects typically require the combined efforts of a variety of specialists. Instead of working in separate offices under separate managers, project participants — whether engineers, financial analysts, marketing professionals or quality control specialists — work together under the guidance of a project manager to complete a project.
Fourth — nonroutine, with unique elements. This is not an either/or issue but a matter of degree. Accomplishing something that has never been done before — building an electric automobile, or landing two mechanical rovers on Mars — requires solving previously unsolved problems and using breakthrough technology. On the other hand, even basic construction projects that involve established sets of routines and procedures require some degree of customisation that makes them unique.
Fifth — specific time, cost and performance requirements. Projects are evaluated according to accomplishment, cost and time spent. These triple constraints impose a higher degree of accountability than is typically found in most jobs. They also highlight one of the primary functions of project management: balancing the trade-offs among time, cost and performance while ultimately satisfying the customer.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
What a project is not
Projects should not be confused with everyday work. A project is not routine, repetitive work. Ordinary daily work typically requires doing the same or similar work over and over, while a project is done only once — a new product or service exists when the project is completed.







Routine, repetitive work
Projects




Taking class notes
Writing a term paper


Daily entering sales receipts into the accounting ledger
Setting up a sales kiosk for a professional accounting meeting


Responding to a supply-chain request
Developing a supply-chain information system


Practising scales on the piano
Writing a new piano piece


Routine manufacture of a portable music player
Designing a player roughly 2 × 4 inches that interfaces with a PC and stores 10,000 songs


Attaching tags on a manufactured product
Wire-tag projects for large retailers



Recognising the difference is important because too often resources can be used up on daily operations, which may not contribute to the longer-range organisation strategies that require innovative new products.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Program versus project
In practice the terms project and program cause confusion. They are often used synonymously.

A program is a group of related projects designed to accomplish a common goal over an extended period of time.

Each project within a program has a project manager. The major differences lie in scale and time span. Individual projects within a program are motivated by the higher program goal, and program goals are closely related to broad strategic organisation goals.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The project manager
Project managers are often stars in their organisation and well compensated.
They develop, or are given, a project charter or scope statement that defines the objectives and parameters of the project. They work with others to create a project schedule and budget that will guide project execution. They need to understand project priorities so they can make independent decisions.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Project uncertainty
Project uncertainty varies according to the extent the project scope is known and stable, and the extent the technology to be used is known and proven.



Project uncertainty as a function of scope and technology

             Predictable Unpredictable Unknown   Known & stable Technology (How) → unknown Project scope (What) → unknown 


Bridges, product extensions, events and marketing campaigns have well-established scopes and use proven technology, which provides predictability for effective planning.Figure redrawn from Larson & Gray, Ch. 1, Figure 1.2 [1].


However, when the project scope and/or technology is not fully known, things become much less predictable and plan-driven methods suffer.
Such was the case for software development projects, where it was estimated that in 1995 American firms and agencies spent $81 billion on cancelled software projects [2]. Fast forward to 2021, and the cost of poor software quality in the United States was estimated to be over $2 trillion because of unsuccessful projects, software failure, and inferior quality legacy systems [3].

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Rolling wave
Fundamentally, Agile PM employs an incremental, iterative process sometimes referred to as a “rolling wave” approach to complete projects.
Instead of trying to plan for everything up front, the scope of the project evolves. The final project design and outcome is not known in great detail and is continuously developed through a series of incremental iterations (waves). Iterations typically last from one to four weeks.



Rolling wave development across five iterations

                Iteration 1Iteration 2Iteration 3 Iteration 4Iteration 5   Project initiationCloseout 


The goal of each iteration is to make tangible progress. Each new iteration subsumes the work of the previous iterations until the project is completed and the customer is satisfied.Figure redrawn from Larson & Gray, Ch. 1, Figure 1.3 [1].


The goal of each iteration is to make tangible progress — defining a key requirement, solving a technical problem, or creating desired features to demonstrate to the customer. At the end of each iteration, progress is reviewed, adjustments are made, and a different iterative cycle begins.
Agile PM focuses on active collaboration between the project team and customer representatives, breaking projects into small functional pieces, and adapting to changing requirements.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
section: It is not simply a question of either/or
text:
It is not simply a question of either/or
Agile methods are often used up front in the defining phase to establish specifications and requirements, and then traditional methods are used to plan, execute and close the project. Agile methods are also used to address certain technical issues on a project while most of the project work is being managed in the traditional way.
Hybrid project management is the name given to this blending of traditional and agile methodologies.
The internal dynamics on Agile projects is quite different from the traditional PM approach. Agile works best in small teams of four to eight members.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
section: Compression of the product life cycle
text:
Compression of the product life cycle
One of the most significant driving forces behind the demand for project management is the shortening of the product life cycle.
Today in high-tech industries the product life cycle is averaging six months to three years. Only 30 years ago, life cycles of 10 to 15 years were not uncommon.
Time-to-market for new products with short life cycles has become increasingly important. A common rule of thumb in the world of high-tech product development is that a six-month project delay can result in a 33 percent loss in product revenue share.
Speed, therefore, becomes a competitive advantage; more and more organisations are relying on cross-functional project teams to get new products and services to the market as quickly as possible.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Knowledge explosion
The growth in new knowledge has increased the complexity of projects, because projects encompass the latest advances.
Building a road 30 years ago was a somewhat simple process. Today each area has increased in complexity — including materials, specifications, codes, aesthetics, equipment and required specialists.
Similarly, in today’s digital, electronic age it is becoming hard to find a new product that does not contain at least one microchip. The same is likely to be true for artificial intelligence.
Product complexity has increased the need to integrate divergent technologies. Project management has emerged as the key discipline for achieving this task.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
section: Triple bottom line — planet, people, profit
text:
Triple bottom line — planet, people, profit
The threat of global warming has brought sustainable business practices to the forefront. Businesses can no longer simply focus on maximising profit to the detriment of the environment and society.
Efforts to reduce carbon imprints and utilise renewable resources are realised through effective project management. The impact of this movement toward sustainability can be seen in changes in the objectives and techniques used to complete projects — for example, achieving a high LEED certification award is often an objective on construction projects.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Small projects represent big problems
The velocity of change required to remain competitive, or simply keep up, has created an organisational climate in which hundreds of projects are implemented concurrently. This climate has created a multiproject environment and a plethora of new problems. Sharing and prioritising resources across a portfolio of projects is a major challenge for senior management.
Many firms have no idea of the problems involved with the inefficient management of small projects:

Small projects typically carry the same or more risk as large projects.
Small projects are perceived as having little impact on the bottom line because they do not demand large amounts of scarce resources and/or money.
Because so many small projects are going on concurrently, and because the perception of the inefficiency impact is small, measuring inefficiency is usually nonexistent.
Many small projects soon add up to large sums of money. Many customers and millions of dollars are lost each year on small projects in product and service organisations.
Small projects can represent hidden costs not measured in the accounting system.

Organisations with many small projects going on concurrently face the most difficult project management problems. A key question becomes one of how to create an organisational environment that supports multiproject management. A process is needed to prioritise and develop a portfolio of small projects that supports the mission of the organisation.
In summary, a variety of environmental forces interacting in today’s business world contribute to the increased demand for good project management across all industries and sectors.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The technical dimension
The technical side is the methodology — planning, scheduling and controlling. It is the orderly half of the job, and it produces documents.
A scope statement is what ties the project to the customer, and it is what makes planning and control possible at all: you cannot control against a target nobody wrote down. From it come the deliverables and the work breakdown structure, which is what you actually plan and monitor against.
The WBS is worth thinking of as a database rather than a diagram. It links every level of the organisation to every major deliverable and to every piece of work, down to the individual tasks in a work package. Because those links are built in, a change anywhere is documented, and can be traced back to whatever caused it. That traceability is the whole payoff, and it is why the structure is worth the effort of building properly.
Being well trained in this half is necessary. It is not sufficient.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
The sociocultural dimension
Where planning is orderly, implementation is not. It is messy, frequently contradictory, and often paradoxical — and no amount of documentation makes it otherwise.
The manager’s task here is to build a project culture that keeps a team working together and personally invested, and that surfaces problems early enough to do something about them. A culture where bad news travels slowly is a culture that will hand you a surprise late, when it is expensive.
Plans do not survive contact with reality. The skill is not avoiding that; it is recognising the departure quickly and deciding whether to steer back to the plan or change direction.
Underneath all of it is a social network the manager has to build deliberately — across stakeholders who hold genuinely different standards, are committed to different things, and see the same project from incompatible angles. None of that is a failure of the people involved. It is the normal condition of the work.

title: Week 1 · Modern Project Management
text:
Master of both
Neither half substitutes for the other, and both have to be actively managed. The practical shape of the job is that you produce a plan and a budget, and at the same time orchestrate the contributions of people you mostly do not control. A manager strong in one half and weak in the other fails — just in a different way each time.
